newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Palladium chaos triggers crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Palladium chaos triggers crisis talks.

text.p: Market makers in the London-based trade in platinum and palladium held crisis talks on Thursday on chaos in their sector where an acute shortage of the rare white metals has driven prices dramatically higher.

Participants, as the session ended, would not say what was decided. They met against a backdrop of delay to Russian supply, a build-up of big fund holdings of metal and what some dealers said was talk in the market of a possibility of a default on delivery of palladium.
"It's a hairy situation...volatility is huge today," said analyst Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group.

Spot palladium prices lurched back and forth, surging to fix at a new peak of $235.00 per ounce in the morning then diving to fix at $210 in the afternoon, back near Wednesday's level. The morning rate was the highest since the market began setting benchmark prices in 1989.
Prices have risen 100 percent since the start of the year as a suspension of shipments from the largest producer, Russia, squeezed the market.
Dealers said it was unclear what action could be taken to cool the situation in palladium - used in electronics, chemicals, dentistry and auto catalystic coverters -- and also in platinum.

Players borrow metal, rather than buy, when they think high prices won't last -- a prospect that could arise when the Russians eventually start exporting again, or if speculative funds liquidate positions.

"The problem was nobody had the stuff to lend and when some people detected this they insisted on delivery of the physical metal, not cash," a senior dealer said. If a firm could not meet its obligation, as a last resort it could be expelled from the market for a period, he added.
The informal market is self-regulated by the London Platinum and Palladium Market association since the two metals are not traded on an exchange, British official regulatory officials said.
The Bank of England looks after the cash market in gold and silver, but has no oversight over platinum or palladium, a spokeswoman said.

Dealers stopped quoting forward rates for palladium on Thursday after the cost of borrowing surged to around 300 percent for one-month metal on Wednesday night. "Now it is purely a spot market," one dealer said.
The lack of Russian supplies has been compounded by speculative buying by investment funds. The U.S. Tiger Fund is said to be holding 1.5 million ounces of palladium.
Funds are reluctant to open the floodgates since each time they dribble out small parcels of the metal, prices start to crumble, one dealer said.
"The funds have to play this very delicately if they are to have a profitable position," he said.
Despite the market turbulence, deliveries against the New York June palladium futures contract, due to expire on June 25, were proceeding normally, exchange officials there said.

Russia supplies 60 percent of world palladium and about 20 percent of platinum, but fiscal and administrative problems and a possible change of marketing strategy led to a suspension of exports last December.
Palladium's sister metal platinum surged to fix at $442 per ounce on Thursday afternoon, the strongest since July 19, 1995.

Users of both the metals had expected Russian shipments to resume by now and had been borrowing metal to cover their needs. Russian officials told Japanese traders on Wednesday that Russian platinum and palladium exports would resume on June 20, but they also said the export licences had still not yet been granted by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations.
The crisis spilled into the gold market, in which lease rates had almost doubled overnight after a surge of borrowing came into that market.
Some dealers said this was on behalf on a New York-based house which had problems in palladium and was defensively covering forward gold positions. Gold prices were stable around $342-343 an ounce.
